writing.exampleCaption: The two ranges have different upper-bound rules.
writing.explanation:
The range `0..3` contains `0`, `1`, and `2`; its upper bound is excluded. The inclusive form `1..=3` also contains `3`. Half-open ranges fit indexing because a length can be used directly as the excluded end. Inclusive ranges are useful when both endpoints belong to the domain.

Half-open ranges make boundaries compose cleanly. In `0..3`, the first value is included and `3` is excluded, so there are exactly three integers. This mirrors a slice whose length is 3: valid positions are 0, 1, and 2, while the length itself is the first position after the slice. Two adjacent spans such as `0..3` and `3..6` meet without overlapping. That is why half-open intervals are common in indexing and iteration.

The inclusive form `1..=3` includes both endpoints and is a natural fit when the domain itself is phrased that way: days one through three, or levels one through three. The syntax is not just decoration. Changing `..` to `..=` alters which values a `for` loop sees and may add one more iteration. Write out the sequence before running whenever an off-by-one error would matter.

Ranges are values that can be passed to operations, but the exact kinds they support depend on their element type. A range does not automatically protect every use of its numbers as indexes; you still need to know the collection length. Change the upper bound in the sample to `0..=3` and predict the extra line, then try a zero-length half-open range such as `3..3` and explain why the loop body does not run.

A range communicates which endpoints belong to an operation. `0..n` includes zero and excludes `n`; `0..=n` includes both ends. For a collection of length `n`, valid indices stop at `n - 1`, so `0..n` matches them exactly when `n` is positive. This is one reason half-open ranges appear often in Rust. The type of a range is not a collection of stored numbers; iteration produces the values as needed.

Write the values generated by `2..5` and `2..=5` before running either loop. Then test an empty range such as `3..3` and explain why its body never runs. For indexing, prefer iterating over items directly when you do not need indices; use `enumerate()` when you need both an index and an item. Boundary reasoning matters more than memorizing one syntax: state clearly whether the end is inside or outside the operation.
writing.feedback: The upper bound of `..` is excluded, so `5` is not part of the range.
